name: EDZNET Security Guard
author: EDZNET

sections.description:
EDZNET Security Guard stops the most common ways WordPress sites are taken over. Step-by-step setup guide: https://edznet.io/blog/edznet-security-guard-plugin-guide

Two-Factor Authentication

Require two-factor authentication (2FA) for administrators. Each administrator chooses how they get their 6-digit code:

  • Authenticator app (recommended): standard TOTP codes (RFC 6238) from Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Microsoft Authenticator or similar, set up by scanning a QR code.
  • Email code: for people who struggle with apps. Codes expire after 10 minutes, five wrong codes end the attempt, and a test code proves the site’s email works first. The plugin says plainly that email codes are less secure than an app, and the site owner can turn them off.

Every administrator also gets 10 single-use backup codes, and app users can opt in to email recovery. You can require 2FA for all administrators or for new ones; anyone who hasn’t set it up yet is walked through it at their next login, so nobody is locked out.

Block Administrator Creation

A compromised admin account often creates a second administrator as a backdoor. While this is on, no user can be created as, or promoted to, Administrator. Existing administrators are unaffected.

Block URL Credentials

Brute-force scripts send credentials in the URL (wp-login.php?log=Ben&pwd=T3m). Any visit to the login page with credentials in the query string gets 403 Forbidden.

Admin Login Alerts

Every administrator login sends an email with the username, IP address, browser and time, so a login you didn’t make stands out. On by default; send them to any address.

Block Accounts

Block any account from logging in with one click on the Users screen; its sessions end at once. Only the first administrator can block another administrator, and the first administrator can never be blocked. Attempts to sign in as a blocked account are logged.

Plugin Audit and Unverified Plugin Blocking

A common attack is to sign in with a stolen password, upload a fake plugin and activate it. Security Guard checks every plugin against the official WordPress.org file checksums and scans plugin code for high-risk techniques (hidden or decoded code, running commands from a request, loading code from a blockchain, hiding from the Plugins screen, heavy obfuscation).

  • New plugins that can’t be verified are blocked from activation until the first administrator approves them in EDZNET Guard > Plugin audit (for example a premium plugin), on the Plugins screen, the REST API and WP-CLI.
  • Plugins already installed are never blocked, only flagged, so turning it on can’t break a working site.
  • Plugins with high-risk code are always blocked until approved, and you are emailed. Approvals are re-checked if the code changes.

The audit runs daily, on every activation and on demand.

Firewall

Security Guard locks out IP addresses that attack the site (EDZNET Guard > Firewall):

  • Failed logins: 5 within 15 minutes lock the address out for an hour (all adjustable), on the login page, XML-RPC, application passwords, login forms such as WooCommerce’s and wrong two-factor codes. Repeat lockouts last twice as long, up to 24 hours; a fifth in one day lasts a week.
  • Usernames bots try first (admin, root, test…) lock the address out at once, when no such account exists.
  • Probes for files only attackers look for (/.env, /.git/config, wp-config.php.bak, phpMyAdmin, web shells) and attack tools such as sqlmap, Nikto and WPScan.
  • Missing-page floods (missing images, styles and fonts don’t count) and author scans (?author=1).
  • Optionally turn off logins over XML-RPC.

By default a locked-out address can’t log in but can still read the site, because many people can share one address; you can block the whole site instead.

It can’t be turned against you: forwarding headers (X-Forwarded-For) are only believed from Cloudflare, your host’s proxy or a proxy you trust, so attackers can’t fake an address. Addresses an administrator used in the last 30 days, your allowlist and signed-in visitors are never blocked, search engines are verified by DNS first, and define( 'EDZNET_GUARD_FW_UNLOCK', true ); in wp-config.php switches it off in an emergency. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Two optional extras, both off by default:

  • Access-log scanning: every 10 minutes the firewall reads the access logs your host already keeps (cPanel’s access-logs folder) and counts what WordPress never sees: probes the web server refused by itself, attack tools reading cached pages and floods of refused requests. It also emails you if a file such as .env, a database dump or debug.log was actually downloaded.
  • Server-level blocking: locked-out IPv4 addresses are also refused in .htaccess (Apache and LiteSpeed), before WordPress or a page cache runs. The site is checked after every change and the rules are removed if anything goes wrong.

With Vulnerability Watch on, you can also opt in to the EDZNET threat list: your site shares the addresses it locked out and blocks addresses that attacked other EDZNET customers’ sites. An address is only listed when three different customers’ sites reported it within a day, and drops off two days after the last report. Administrator addresses are never listed, and listed addresses are only kept from logging in unless you choose the whole site.

Disk space

A full hosting disk breaks a site in confusing ways (“your session has expired”, failed uploads). EDZNET Guard > Disk space shows where the space goes and emails you at 85% and 95% full.

Vulnerability Watch (with an EDZNET Geo API Pro key)

Checks your WordPress version, plugins and themes against a daily-updated database of known vulnerabilities, twice a day and after every update, rated critical to low with the version that fixes each one. Email alerts for critical and high findings, a site risk score and a dashboard widget. One site per EDZNET Geo API Pro key (https://edznet.io/api-services); without a key you can choose a free count of known vulnerabilities. Nothing is sent until the first administrator turns one on; see External Services below.

First Administrator Lock

Every setting, including two-factor authentication, can only be changed by the first administrator, so a compromised admin account cannot quietly weaken the protections.

Comment and Content Controls

  • Disable comments site-wide, close comments on every existing post in one click, or delete all pending comments.
  • Hide post authors, post dates and the “Comments are closed” text on the front end.

Go Further: EDZNET Geolocation

With our EDZNET Geolocation plugin you can block countries, only allow logins from chosen countries and block individual IPs, and admin login alerts show where the login came from. https://wordpress.org/plugins/edznet-geolocation/

The protections, alerts and toggles work straight after activation. Two-factor authentication is off until you turn it on.

Source Code

Every PHP, JavaScript and CSS file is the original, human-readable source: nothing is minified, compiled or bundled, and there is no build step. The only third-party file is the QR-code library below, shipped unminified.

Third-Party Libraries

  • qrcode.js (js/qrcode.js) — by davidshimjs, based on the “QR Code for JavaScript” library by Kazuhiko Arase. Licensed under the MIT license. Upstream: https://github.com/davidshimjs/qrcodejs. Shipped unmodified and unminified; used to draw the TOTP enrollment QR code in the browser so that no secret ever leaves the site.

External Services

WordPress.org plugin checksums. To verify installed plugins, the plugin audit requests the published checksums for each installed plugin from WordPress.org: https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin-checksums/<plugin-slug>/<version>.json. Only the plugin’s folder name (slug) and version number are sent, as part of the URL. No information about your site, its users or its visitors is sent. Requests are made when the audit runs (daily, when a plugin is activated, and when you click “Run audit now”), and results are cached. This service is provided by WordPress.org: terms https://wordpress.org/about/domains/ and privacy policy https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/.

Login locations (only with EDZNET Geolocation). If the separate EDZNET Geolocation plugin is active and configured, the IP address of an administrator who signs in is looked up through that plugin’s own geolocation service so the login alert can show its location. Security Guard makes no request of its own for this; see the EDZNET Geolocation plugin for details of that service. Without EDZNET Geolocation, no IP address is sent anywhere.

Official EDZNET must-use plugins (only when one is installed). If a must-use plugin in wp-content/mu-plugins presents itself as the EDZNET Hands-Off Agent (which EDZNET installs on managed websites), the plugin audit downloads the list of official EDZNET build fingerprints from https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/official and compares it with a fingerprint of the file worked out on your site. Nothing is sent except the request itself (no site address, plugin list or user data). It is checked at most once a day, and never on sites without such a plugin. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

EDZNET Vulnerability Watch (only when you turn it on). This is EDZNET’s own service at edznet.io, used only after the first administrator turns on Vulnerability Watch or the free count on the EDZNET Guard > Vulnerability Watch screen.

  • Turning on Vulnerability Watch sends your Geo API Pro key, your site’s address, a random install ID and a one-time secret to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/activate. edznet.io then calls your site once at <your site>/?rest_route=/edznet-guard/v1/verify with a random challenge, and the plugin answers with a code made from that one-time secret. This confirms the request came from your site. The route answers only while an activation is in progress.
  • Each check sends your site’s address, its WordPress version, and the folder name (slug) and version number of each installed plugin and theme to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/check, with the site’s own token. Checks run twice a day, a minute after you install or update WordPress, a plugin or a theme, and when you click “Check now”.
  • The free count sends the same WordPress version and plugin and theme slugs and versions, without your site’s address, to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/summary once a day and when you click “Count again”.
  • Turning Vulnerability Watch off tells https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/release to free the key.

No information about your users, visitors, content or settings is sent. The vulnerability data is provided to EDZNET by Wordfence Intelligence, and each finding shows its source and copyright notice. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

EDZNET threat list (only when you turn it on). This is EDZNET’s own service at edznet.io, available while Vulnerability Watch is on, used only after the first administrator ticks “Share attacking addresses with EDZNET and block the EDZNET threat list” on EDZNET Guard > Firewall.

  • Every hour the site sends to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/threats/report, with its Vulnerability Watch site token and address: the IP addresses its firewall locked out since the last report, each with the reason (failed logins, probes, missing-page floods), how many times and when; the addresses the site owner unlocked; and, once a day, the addresses administrators logged in from in the last 30 days, so that they are never listed. No usernames, passwords, user agents or page addresses are sent.
  • It then downloads the changes to the shared list from https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/threats/list.

EDZNET keeps each report for 7 days and lists an address only when sites of three different EDZNET customers reported it within 24 hours; it drops off 48 hours after the last report. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

Two-factor codes are generated and verified entirely on your own server, and the QR code is drawn in the browser by the bundled qrcode.js. Emailed codes are sent with your site’s own wp_mail(), stored only as a keyed hash, and backup codes are stored hashed like passwords.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the edznet-security-guard folder to /wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate the plugin through the Plugins screen in WordPress.
  3. The protections are now active. Review them under EDZNET Guard in the admin menu.
sections.faq:
Is it compatible with WordPress 7.2 and PHP 8.6?

Yes. It is tested with WordPress 7.2 and PHP 8.6, with debug logging on and no warnings. It still works back to WordPress 5.8 and PHP 7.2.

Which account can change the settings?

The site’s first administrator account — the user with the Administrator role and the earliest registration date (registration dates are not changed when an account is renamed). If that account is deleted, the lock moves to the next earliest-registered administrator.

My host manages my site. Can their account own the settings?

Yes. A managed-hosting tool can name its own administrator account as the owner with the edznet_guard_first_admin_id filter (only an existing administrator is accepted). Your own administrator account keeps working as normal; only the locked Security Guard settings are then changed by your host. EDZNET Hands-Off sites work this way.

I’m an admin but the settings are locked. Why?

Only the first administrator account can change these settings. This is intentional: a compromised admin account should not be able to disable the protections.

Can the first administrator create new admins?

Yes — temporarily disable “Block administrator creation”, create the account, then re-enable it.

Does this work with REST API or XML-RPC user creation?

Yes. The block is enforced at the core wp_insert_user() level, so admin-created users, REST API calls, and XML-RPC requests are all refused while the setting is enabled.

What triggers an admin login alert?

Any successful sign-in by a user with the Administrator role — including the first administrator. Each alert includes the username, display name, IP address, browser, the time of the login (with timezone) and whether a two-factor code was verified. Alerts are sent to the first administrator’s email unless you set a different address on the settings page.

On sites with several administrators, the wording depends on who signed in. When the alert is about your own login it says “If this was you, no action is needed”. When it is about another administrator it names them and explains how to check with them, block the account and reset its password if the login wasn’t expected.

How does two-factor authentication work?

Once enabled, an administrator enters their username and password as usual, then a 6-digit code: either from an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Microsoft Authenticator, and any other TOTP-compatible app), or emailed to them, depending on the method they chose. App codes are generated from a secret that is only shown once, as a QR code or a text key, and refresh every 30 seconds. Emailed codes work once and expire after 10 minutes.

Should I use email codes or an authenticator app?

An app if you can. Email codes are only as safe as the mailbox: anyone who can get into it, and knows the password, can sign in. They are still far better than no second step, because they stop the most common attack, signing in with a stolen or reused password. If email codes aren’t wanted on a site, the first administrator can untick “Email codes” on the settings page.

What are backup codes?

Ten single-use codes (like k7mq-2xpa) shown once when two-factor authentication is set up. Each one signs you in once if you can’t get a code (“Use a backup code” on the login step). Save them in a password manager or print them. You can make a new set from your profile at any time, which cancels the old ones.

Where does an administrator set up two-factor authentication?

In their profile under “EDZNET Guard — Two-Factor Authentication”, or on the login page itself: an administrator who hasn’t set up 2FA yet is shown the enrollment screen at their next login instead of being signed straight in.

I lost my phone / authenticator app. How do I sign in?

Use one of your backup codes, or, if you turned on email recovery in your profile, choose “Can’t use your app? Email me a code” on the login step. Then set up the app again from your profile.

Otherwise the first administrator can open the administrator’s profile and reset (remove) their two-factor authentication, then they sign in again and set up a new secret. If the locked-out administrator IS the first administrator, the secret can be removed with one click from their own profile by an administrator who has already completed 2FA — or, if nobody can get in, the two-factor authentication can be turned off directly in the database by deleting the edznet_guard_2fa_enabled option.

What is Vulnerability Watch and what does it cost?

It checks the WordPress version, plugins and themes on your site against a database of known vulnerabilities and tells you what to fix. It comes with an EDZNET Geo API Pro key, which also covers geolocation lookups (https://edznet.io/api-services). Each key covers Vulnerability Watch on one site; the free count needs no key.

Does Vulnerability Watch work on a staging copy of my site?

No. A copy on another address is recognised as a copy and stops using the live site’s key, so your live site keeps being checked. Use a separate key for a staging site that needs its own checks.

How do I move Vulnerability Watch to another site?

Click “Turn off” on the old site, or release the key from your Geo API Pro service in the EDZNET client area, then turn it on on the new site. A key that hasn’t been used for 60 days is freed automatically.

I locked myself out. How do I get back in?

Addresses you have logged in from as an administrator in the last 30 days are never locked out, so this is rare. If it happens, add define( 'EDZNET_GUARD_FW_UNLOCK', true ); to wp-config.php, log in, unlock your address on EDZNET Guard > Firewall, then remove the line. Locks also expire on their own (an hour by default). The same line also removes the firewall’s rules from .htaccess when server-level blocking is on.

My site is behind a CDN or proxy. Does the firewall see the real visitor?

Cloudflare is recognised automatically. For any other proxy, CDN or load balancer, add its addresses under Trusted proxies on the Firewall page. When an administrator logs in through a proxy that isn’t listed, the Firewall page shows a warning with a “Trust this proxy” button.

What does access-log scanning read, and does it work on my host?

It reads the web server’s access logs for your site, which your host already keeps: on cPanel hosting the files in the access-logs folder of your account. Only new lines are read, every 10 minutes, and nothing from them is kept except the firewall’s counters. The Firewall page shows which logs were found and whether they can be read. Other hosts can point the plugin at their logs with the edznet_guard_fw_log_files filter. If your logs record a proxy’s address rather than the visitor’s (some CDN setups), the page says so and those lines are never counted.

Is it safe to let the plugin write to .htaccess?

The plugin only adds its own block, marked # BEGIN EDZNET Guard Firewall / # END EDZNET Guard Firewall, at the top of the file, and never changes anything else. It uses mod_rewrite rules rather than access rules, so it can’t weaken another plugin’s IP bans or an “only my IP may log in” rule. After every change the plugin loads your home page and login page, and if either fails the block is removed and the option turned off. It is removed when you turn the option off or deactivate the plugin. If you ever delete the plugin folder by hand, you can delete that block from .htaccess yourself. It isn’t offered behind a proxy or CDN, where the web server can’t see visitors’ addresses.

I got an email that a sensitive file can be downloaded. What should I do?

Delete the file named in the email, or move it out of the website folder, as soon as possible. Files like .env, database dumps and debug.log can contain passwords, keys and personal data. Then change any passwords or keys the file contained. The plugin only sends this email after fetching the file itself and confirming it isn’t just a “page not found” page.

What is the EDZNET threat list and what does it share?

An opt-in list of attacking IP addresses shared between EDZNET customers’ sites (it needs Vulnerability Watch, which comes with an EDZNET Geo API Pro key). When it is on, your site sends EDZNET the addresses its firewall locked out (with the reason, count and times), the addresses you unlocked, and the addresses administrators log in from. It downloads the list every hour and keeps listed addresses from logging in. An address is listed only when three different customers’ sites reported it within a day, and drops off two days after the last report. Administrator addresses, Google and Bing crawlers and EDZNET’s own servers are never listed, and your “Never lock out” list always wins. Nothing is sent until the first administrator turns it on.

Does the firewall slow the site down?

No. Checking a request reads one small list that WordPress has already loaded; the database is only written when something suspicious happens (a failed login, a probe or a missing page). Access-log scanning runs in the background every 10 minutes and reads at most 5 MB per run, and server-level blocking makes an attack cheaper for the server, because refused requests never start WordPress.

Does this plugin offer geo-blocking?

Not built in — but it pairs with our EDZNET Geolocation plugin, which blocks whole countries or continents from your site’s pages, can limit logins to the countries you choose (wp-login.php, other login forms, XML-RPC and application passwords), blocks individual IPs, and shows where comments, logins and registrations come from. When Geolocation is active, Security Guard links straight to its country-blocking screen. Install it from WordPress.org.

How do I block a user from logging in?

On the Users screen, hover over a user and click Block login. The account is refused at the login screen and its existing sessions are ended. Click Unblock login (or the button on the EDZNET Guard settings page) to restore it at any time.

Can I block an administrator?

Yes. Any administrator can block a non-admin account; only the site’s first administrator can block another administrator. The first administrator’s own account can never be blocked, so the site owner can’t be locked out.

Can I see who tried to log in with a blocked account?

Yes. Every attempt is recorded on the EDZNET Guard settings page under Blocked login attempts — username, email, IP address, browser and time, newest first (up to the last 100).

Can I turn off the admin login alerts?

Yes. Untick “Email me when an administrator logs in” on the EDZNET Guard settings page. The toggle is locked to the first administrator like the other settings.

Who can use the comment controls?

Only the site’s first administrator. “Disable comments globally” is a protected setting, and the “Close commenting on all posts” and “Delete all pending comments” buttons are locked the same way so a compromised admin account cannot purge comments or weaken moderation.

Does disabling comments globally delete existing comments?

No. It only hides comment forms and makes new posts default to closed. To change existing posts, use “Close commenting on all posts”. To remove comments that are waiting for moderation, use “Delete all pending comments”.

How do the “hide author”, “hide date” and “hide comment closed text” toggles work?

They are front-end filters and CSS rules. Hidden content is removed from the markup the theme outputs, and a small stylesheet hides common author/date/comment-closed elements. Because themes structure their post meta differently, these are a best-effort helper for most themes rather than a guarantee for every theme.

Do the front-end toggles affect the admin?

No. Hiding post authors, dates and comment-closed text only affects the front end of the site. The admin screens always show full author and date information.
sections.changelog:
2.2.0

  • New: the EDZNET threat list (EDZNET Guard > Firewall, off by default, needs Vulnerability Watch). Your site shares the addresses it locked out and blocks addresses that attacked other EDZNET customers’ sites. An address is listed only when three different customers’ sites reported it within a day, drops off two days after the last report, and is never listed if any site reported it as an administrator’s address. Listed addresses are kept from logging in (or from the whole site, if you choose); your allowlist and signed-in visitors always win. The refusal message tells a listed visitor why.
  • The list is checked with one database lookup and only where a refusal can happen; it is kept in its own table and updated hourly with changes only.
  • New: a Guide link on the Plugins screen and on every EDZNET Guard page, to the step-by-step setup guide.

2.1.0

  • New: access-log scanning (EDZNET Guard > Firewall, off by default). Every 10 minutes the firewall reads the new lines of the site’s access logs (cPanel access-logs) and counts what WordPress never sees: probes the web server refused by itself (/.env, /.git/…), attack tools reading cached pages and floods of refused requests. Lines from Cloudflare, trusted proxies and private addresses are never counted, and old lines are never counted when it is turned on.
  • New: an email when a sensitive file (.env, .git/config, wp-config backups, database dumps, debug.log) was actually downloaded from the site. The plugin fetches the file itself first, so “page not found” pages don’t cause false alarms. Nothing of the file is stored.
  • New: server-level blocking (off by default, Apache and LiteSpeed). Locked-out IPv4 addresses are refused in .htaccess before WordPress or a page cache runs; with “The whole site” this also covers cached pages. Uses mod_rewrite rules at the top of .htaccess, so other plugins’ IP bans and login allowlists are never weakened; signed-in visitors are passed on to WordPress. The home and login pages are checked after every change and the block is removed if either fails. Unlocks take effect at once.
  • The emergency switch EDZNET_GUARD_FW_UNLOCK also removes the .htaccess rules.

2.0.0

  • New: Firewall (EDZNET Guard > Firewall). Locks out IP addresses after repeated failed logins (login page, XML-RPC, application passwords, login forms, wrong two-factor codes), at once for usernames bots try first (admin, root, test… when no such account exists), after probes for sensitive files (/.env, /.git, wp-config backups, phpMyAdmin, web shells) or attack tools (sqlmap, Nikto, WPScan…), and after floods of missing-page requests. Lockouts double for repeat offenders. Blocks logins only (default) or the whole site.
  • New: stop ?author=N username scans; optionally turn off logins over XML-RPC.
  • New: lockout log, locked-out list with Unlock, 30-day totals, optional email on lockout, allowlist, trusted proxies, emergency switch EDZNET_GUARD_FW_UNLOCK.
  • Security: the visitor IP in admin login alerts and the blocked-login log was taken from the X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP headers, which anyone can send. Those headers are now only believed from Cloudflare, a private (host) address or a trusted proxy.
  • Privacy: Settings > Privacy > Policy Guide (under “EDZNET Security Guard”) now suggests wording for your privacy policy about the IP addresses the firewall records (counters deleted after 7 days without activity, lockout log limited to the latest 200 entries, nothing sent anywhere).

1.9.1

  • Changed: Disk space no longer reads or shows the server’s own disk. On shared hosting that is the host’s whole server, not your account, so the figure was misleading. The percentage and alerts now come only from your hosting account’s quota (when your host provides it) or the disk limit you enter.

1.9.0

  • New: Disk space (EDZNET Guard > Disk space). Shows how much hosting space the site uses and where it goes: website files, database, uploads, cache, left-over cache folders, backups kept in wp-content and log files. Measured twice a day.
  • New: an email to the alert address when the hosting space is 85% and again at 95% full. A full disk stops WordPress saving uploads, sessions and cache files, which shows up as errors such as “your session has expired” on forms.
  • Enter your hosting plan’s disk limit for an accurate percentage. Hosts can supply the account’s real quota with the edznet_guard_disk_quota filter.

1.8.2

  • Fixed: right after the EDZNET Hands-Off Agent updated itself, the plugin audit could flag the new version as “does not match any official EDZNET build”, because the list of official builds was cached for a day. An unrecognised agent now makes the audit fetch the list again (at most every 5 minutes) before flagging it.

1.8.1

  • New: the plugin audit recognises the official EDZNET Hands-Off Agent. A copy that matches an official EDZNET build (checked against edznet.io) shows as “Official EDZNET (verified)” with what it does, instead of the “Creates user accounts with the Administrator role” warning. A must-use plugin that claims to be the Hands-Off Agent but matches no official build is flagged as critical and emailed, because a real backdoor could borrow the name.

1.8.0

  • New: email codes as a second two-factor method, for administrators who find authenticator apps hard. Each administrator chooses app or email when they set up 2FA (on the login page or in their profile). Codes expire after 10 minutes, five wrong codes end the login attempt, a new code can be sent after a minute, and a test code proves the site’s email works before it is switched on. Email codes are labelled as less secure than an app wherever they are offered, and the first administrator can turn them off (“Email codes” on the settings page, on by default).
  • New: 10 single-use backup codes for every administrator with 2FA, shown once at setup, with “Use a backup code” on the login step and “Create new backup codes” in the profile.
  • New: optional email recovery for app users (off unless the administrator turns it on in their profile): “Can’t use your app? Email me a code” on the login step.
  • New: five wrong codes now end a two-factor login attempt (authenticator codes included).
  • Code emails say where the sign-in came from (IP address plus city, region, country and provider when EDZNET Geolocation is active with a key), like the admin login alerts.
  • Improved: admin login alerts say whether the sign-in was verified with an authenticator code, an emailed code or a backup code (with how many are left).
  • The site risk score counts administrators who use email codes as having two-factor login.

1.7.2

  • New (for managed hosting): the edznet_guard_first_admin_id filter sets which administrator owns the protected settings (only an existing administrator, or super admin on multisite, is accepted), edznet_guard_locked_notice changes the “Settings locked” text so it can say who manages the site, and edznet_guard_allow_admin_grant lets trusted code give its own management account the Administrator role while “Block administrator creation” is on. Both are off unless something uses them; nothing changes for other sites.

1.7.1

  • Readme: EDZNET Geolocation 1.6 adds login protection (only allow logins from chosen countries), so the geo-blocking notes now mention it.
  • Readme: a Vulnerability Watch key can also be released from the Geo API Pro service in the EDZNET client area.

1.7.0

  • New: Vulnerability Watch (EDZNET Guard > Vulnerability Watch). With an EDZNET Geo API Pro key, Security Guard checks your WordPress version, plugins and themes against a database of known vulnerabilities, updated daily, twice a day and after every update. Findings show their severity and the version that fixes them, affected plugins are marked on the Plugins screen, and new critical and high-risk findings are emailed to you.
  • New: site risk score and dashboard widget, combining known vulnerabilities with the Plugin audit, two-factor login, waiting updates and the number of administrators.
  • New: without a key, an optional free count of the known vulnerabilities affecting your site.
  • Readme: EDZNET Geolocation blocks countries from your site’s pages; it does not block the login page by country, as the readme said before.

1.6.0

  • New: WordPress Multisite support. Network-activate the plugin and manage login protection, two-factor authentication, admin login alerts, blocked accounts and the Plugin audit from Network Admin. They are owned by the network’s first super admin, with one daily audit for the whole network. Comment and front-end settings stay on each site’s own page.
  • New: on a network, unverified plugins stay blocked for site administrators too, and 2FA and login alerts cover the administrators of every site, whichever site’s login page they use.
  • Fix: “Block administrator creation” now works. It never actually blocked new administrators before, because it checked a field WordPress doesn’t pass. It now blocks every way of granting the Administrator role (Users screens, REST API, WP-CLI and other plugins). If you need to add an administrator, the first administrator must turn the setting off first. Existing administrators are not affected.

1.5.3

  • Fix: old Elementor build files named after a widget (for example assets/js/accordion.d0e98fa492444fcce9f9.bundle.js) are now also recognised as leftovers from earlier versions, so they no longer mark the plugin as modified.

1.5.2

  • Fix: the Plugin audit no longer flags long encoded strings that are only data, such as the Unicode line-break table in html2canvas (bundled with Elementor Pro). A string is reported when it decodes or unpacks to readable code, or when the same file runs code built at runtime.
  • Fix: old JavaScript build files left behind by earlier updates (for example Elementor’s hashed assets/js/*.bundle.js files) no longer mark a plugin as modified. They are still scanned for risky code, and the audit lists how many there are.

1.5.1

  • Fix: deleting a plugin now clears its Plugin audit warning straight away. Before, the warning stayed on the Plugins screen and dashboard until the next audit ran. Installing or updating a plugin also re-checks it immediately.

1.5.0

  • New: plugin audit. Every plugin is checked against WordPress.org’s published file checksums and scanned for high-risk code (hidden or decoded code, commands from web requests, blockchain-loaded scripts, plugins that hide themselves, obfuscation). Results are on the new EDZNET Guard > Plugin audit screen and on the Plugins screen.
  • New: plugins that can’t be verified against WordPress.org are blocked from activation until the first administrator approves them. Plugins installed before this version, and EDZNET plugins, are only flagged, never blocked. Plugins with high-risk code are always blocked until approved, and the alert address is emailed when one is found.
  • New: with EDZNET Geolocation active, admin login alerts show the location and internet provider of the IP address.

1.4.4

  • Fix: admin notices from other plugins (for example review or upgrade prompts) were displayed inside the EDZNET Security Guard settings page header. They now appear below it.

1.4.3

  • Improved: admin login alert emails are now worded for multi-administrator sites. An alert about another administrator names them and explains how to confirm the login with them, block the account and reset its password, instead of telling the recipient “If this was you, no action is needed”. Alerts about your own login keep the “if this was you” wording.
  • Improved: login alerts now show the time with its timezone and whether the sign-in was verified with a two-factor code.
  • New: refreshed settings page with a branded header, a status bar and settings grouped into cards (Login protection, Two-factor authentication, Comments, Front-end content).
  • Tweak: the “Delete all pending comments” confirmation moved from an inline onsubmit attribute into the enqueued js/admin.js.

1.4.2

  • Removed the site-wide “EDZNET Geolocation” admin notice. The companion-plugin recommendation now appears only on the plugin’s own EDZNET Guard settings page, so no other admin screen is touched.
  • All admin and login-screen CSS moved out of PHP into css/admin.css and css/login.css, and all JavaScript into js/qr-init.js and js/profile-2fa.js, loaded via wp_enqueue_style() / wp_enqueue_script(). No inline style attributes remain in the plugin’s markup.
  • Hardening: every admin_post handler (block/unblock account, clear blocked-login log, two-factor setup/removal) now verifies the nonce first and then re-checks current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) explicitly, instead of relying only on the first-administrator identity check.
  • The Users-screen notices are now gated on the list_users capability.
  • Documented in the readme that the plugin ships complete unminified source with no build step, credited the bundled MIT-licensed qrcode.js library, and stated explicitly that the plugin contacts no external service.

1.4.1

  • Security and UI fixes.

1.4.0

  • Added two-factor authentication for administrators (TOTP / RFC 6238, works with Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password and more). QR-code or text-key enrollment from the profile or the login page, optional “require for all admins”, “force new admins to enroll”, and “force enrollment on next login” toggles. Locked to the first administrator.
  • Added account blocking: “Block login” / “Unblock login” row actions on the Users screen, able to block administrator accounts (first administrator only), with immediate session termination and a log of every attempted sign-in by blocked accounts.
  • Added a recommendation for the companion EDZNET Geolocation plugin (geo-blocking by country and visitor tracking), with direct links to its blocking screen once it’s installed.

1.3.0

  • Added admin login alerts: emails the first administrator (or a custom address) with the username, IP address, browser and time whenever an administrator signs in. On by default, locked to the first administrator.

1.2.0

  • Added front-end content tuning: “Hide post authors”, “Hide post dates” and “Hide comment closed text” toggles, each independent and locked to the first administrator.

1.1.0

  • Added “Disable comments globally” toggle (hides front-end comment forms, new posts default to closed).
  • Added “Close commenting on all posts” bulk action.
  • Added “Delete all pending comments” danger action. All comment controls are locked to the first administrator.

1.0.0

  • Initial release. Blocks creation/promotion of administrator accounts and refuses login attempts that pass credentials through the URL. Settings locked to the site’s first administrator.

short_description: Requires 2FA for administrators, blocks new admin creation, refuses URL-credential logins, and emails you on admin logins. Locked to first admin.
description:
EDZNET Security Guard stops the most common ways WordPress sites are taken over. Step-by-step setup guide: https://edznet.io/blog/edznet-security-guard-plugin-guide

Two-Factor Authentication

Require two-factor authentication (2FA) for administrators. Each administrator chooses how they get their 6-digit code:

  • Authenticator app (recommended): standard TOTP codes (RFC 6238) from Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Microsoft Authenticator or similar, set up by scanning a QR code.
  • Email code: for people who struggle with apps. Codes expire after 10 minutes, five wrong codes end the attempt, and a test code proves the site’s email works first. The plugin says plainly that email codes are less secure than an app, and the site owner can turn them off.

Every administrator also gets 10 single-use backup codes, and app users can opt in to email recovery. You can require 2FA for all administrators or for new ones; anyone who hasn’t set it up yet is walked through it at their next login, so nobody is locked out.

Block Administrator Creation

A compromised admin account often creates a second administrator as a backdoor. While this is on, no user can be created as, or promoted to, Administrator. Existing administrators are unaffected.

Block URL Credentials

Brute-force scripts send credentials in the URL (wp-login.php?log=Ben&pwd=T3m). Any visit to the login page with credentials in the query string gets 403 Forbidden.

Admin Login Alerts

Every administrator login sends an email with the username, IP address, browser and time, so a login you didn’t make stands out. On by default; send them to any address.

Block Accounts

Block any account from logging in with one click on the Users screen; its sessions end at once. Only the first administrator can block another administrator, and the first administrator can never be blocked. Attempts to sign in as a blocked account are logged.

Plugin Audit and Unverified Plugin Blocking

A common attack is to sign in with a stolen password, upload a fake plugin and activate it. Security Guard checks every plugin against the official WordPress.org file checksums and scans plugin code for high-risk techniques (hidden or decoded code, running commands from a request, loading code from a blockchain, hiding from the Plugins screen, heavy obfuscation).

  • New plugins that can’t be verified are blocked from activation until the first administrator approves them in EDZNET Guard > Plugin audit (for example a premium plugin), on the Plugins screen, the REST API and WP-CLI.
  • Plugins already installed are never blocked, only flagged, so turning it on can’t break a working site.
  • Plugins with high-risk code are always blocked until approved, and you are emailed. Approvals are re-checked if the code changes.

The audit runs daily, on every activation and on demand.

Firewall

Security Guard locks out IP addresses that attack the site (EDZNET Guard > Firewall):

  • Failed logins: 5 within 15 minutes lock the address out for an hour (all adjustable), on the login page, XML-RPC, application passwords, login forms such as WooCommerce’s and wrong two-factor codes. Repeat lockouts last twice as long, up to 24 hours; a fifth in one day lasts a week.
  • Usernames bots try first (admin, root, test…) lock the address out at once, when no such account exists.
  • Probes for files only attackers look for (/.env, /.git/config, wp-config.php.bak, phpMyAdmin, web shells) and attack tools such as sqlmap, Nikto and WPScan.
  • Missing-page floods (missing images, styles and fonts don’t count) and author scans (?author=1).
  • Optionally turn off logins over XML-RPC.

By default a locked-out address can’t log in but can still read the site, because many people can share one address; you can block the whole site instead.

It can’t be turned against you: forwarding headers (X-Forwarded-For) are only believed from Cloudflare, your host’s proxy or a proxy you trust, so attackers can’t fake an address. Addresses an administrator used in the last 30 days, your allowlist and signed-in visitors are never blocked, search engines are verified by DNS first, and define( 'EDZNET_GUARD_FW_UNLOCK', true ); in wp-config.php switches it off in an emergency. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Two optional extras, both off by default:

  • Access-log scanning: every 10 minutes the firewall reads the access logs your host already keeps (cPanel’s access-logs folder) and counts what WordPress never sees: probes the web server refused by itself, attack tools reading cached pages and floods of refused requests. It also emails you if a file such as .env, a database dump or debug.log was actually downloaded.
  • Server-level blocking: locked-out IPv4 addresses are also refused in .htaccess (Apache and LiteSpeed), before WordPress or a page cache runs. The site is checked after every change and the rules are removed if anything goes wrong.

With Vulnerability Watch on, you can also opt in to the EDZNET threat list: your site shares the addresses it locked out and blocks addresses that attacked other EDZNET customers’ sites. An address is only listed when three different customers’ sites reported it within a day, and drops off two days after the last report. Administrator addresses are never listed, and listed addresses are only kept from logging in unless you choose the whole site.

Disk space

A full hosting disk breaks a site in confusing ways (“your session has expired”, failed uploads). EDZNET Guard > Disk space shows where the space goes and emails you at 85% and 95% full.

Vulnerability Watch (with an EDZNET Geo API Pro key)

Checks your WordPress version, plugins and themes against a daily-updated database of known vulnerabilities, twice a day and after every update, rated critical to low with the version that fixes each one. Email alerts for critical and high findings, a site risk score and a dashboard widget. One site per EDZNET Geo API Pro key (https://edznet.io/api-services); without a key you can choose a free count of known vulnerabilities. Nothing is sent until the first administrator turns one on; see External Services below.

First Administrator Lock

Every setting, including two-factor authentication, can only be changed by the first administrator, so a compromised admin account cannot quietly weaken the protections.

Comment and Content Controls

  • Disable comments site-wide, close comments on every existing post in one click, or delete all pending comments.
  • Hide post authors, post dates and the “Comments are closed” text on the front end.

Go Further: EDZNET Geolocation

With our EDZNET Geolocation plugin you can block countries, only allow logins from chosen countries and block individual IPs, and admin login alerts show where the login came from. https://wordpress.org/plugins/edznet-geolocation/

The protections, alerts and toggles work straight after activation. Two-factor authentication is off until you turn it on.

Source Code

Every PHP, JavaScript and CSS file is the original, human-readable source: nothing is minified, compiled or bundled, and there is no build step. The only third-party file is the QR-code library below, shipped unminified.

Third-Party Libraries

  • qrcode.js (js/qrcode.js) — by davidshimjs, based on the “QR Code for JavaScript” library by Kazuhiko Arase. Licensed under the MIT license. Upstream: https://github.com/davidshimjs/qrcodejs. Shipped unmodified and unminified; used to draw the TOTP enrollment QR code in the browser so that no secret ever leaves the site.

External Services

WordPress.org plugin checksums. To verify installed plugins, the plugin audit requests the published checksums for each installed plugin from WordPress.org: https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin-checksums/<plugin-slug>/<version>.json. Only the plugin’s folder name (slug) and version number are sent, as part of the URL. No information about your site, its users or its visitors is sent. Requests are made when the audit runs (daily, when a plugin is activated, and when you click “Run audit now”), and results are cached. This service is provided by WordPress.org: terms https://wordpress.org/about/domains/ and privacy policy https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/.

Login locations (only with EDZNET Geolocation). If the separate EDZNET Geolocation plugin is active and configured, the IP address of an administrator who signs in is looked up through that plugin’s own geolocation service so the login alert can show its location. Security Guard makes no request of its own for this; see the EDZNET Geolocation plugin for details of that service. Without EDZNET Geolocation, no IP address is sent anywhere.

Official EDZNET must-use plugins (only when one is installed). If a must-use plugin in wp-content/mu-plugins presents itself as the EDZNET Hands-Off Agent (which EDZNET installs on managed websites), the plugin audit downloads the list of official EDZNET build fingerprints from https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/official and compares it with a fingerprint of the file worked out on your site. Nothing is sent except the request itself (no site address, plugin list or user data). It is checked at most once a day, and never on sites without such a plugin. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

EDZNET Vulnerability Watch (only when you turn it on). This is EDZNET’s own service at edznet.io, used only after the first administrator turns on Vulnerability Watch or the free count on the EDZNET Guard > Vulnerability Watch screen.

  • Turning on Vulnerability Watch sends your Geo API Pro key, your site’s address, a random install ID and a one-time secret to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/activate. edznet.io then calls your site once at <your site>/?rest_route=/edznet-guard/v1/verify with a random challenge, and the plugin answers with a code made from that one-time secret. This confirms the request came from your site. The route answers only while an activation is in progress.
  • Each check sends your site’s address, its WordPress version, and the folder name (slug) and version number of each installed plugin and theme to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/check, with the site’s own token. Checks run twice a day, a minute after you install or update WordPress, a plugin or a theme, and when you click “Check now”.
  • The free count sends the same WordPress version and plugin and theme slugs and versions, without your site’s address, to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/summary once a day and when you click “Count again”.
  • Turning Vulnerability Watch off tells https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/release to free the key.

No information about your users, visitors, content or settings is sent. The vulnerability data is provided to EDZNET by Wordfence Intelligence, and each finding shows its source and copyright notice. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

EDZNET threat list (only when you turn it on). This is EDZNET’s own service at edznet.io, available while Vulnerability Watch is on, used only after the first administrator ticks “Share attacking addresses with EDZNET and block the EDZNET threat list” on EDZNET Guard > Firewall.

  • Every hour the site sends to https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/threats/report, with its Vulnerability Watch site token and address: the IP addresses its firewall locked out since the last report, each with the reason (failed logins, probes, missing-page floods), how many times and when; the addresses the site owner unlocked; and, once a day, the addresses administrators logged in from in the last 30 days, so that they are never listed. No usernames, passwords, user agents or page addresses are sent.
  • It then downloads the changes to the shared list from https://edznet.io/api/guard/v1/threats/list.

EDZNET keeps each report for 7 days and lists an address only when sites of three different EDZNET customers reported it within 24 hours; it drops off 48 hours after the last report. Terms: https://edznet.io/terms-of-service.php. Privacy policy: https://edznet.io/privacy-policy.php.

Two-factor codes are generated and verified entirely on your own server, and the QR code is drawn in the browser by the bundled qrcode.js. Emailed codes are sent with your site’s own wp_mail(), stored only as a keyed hash, and backup codes are stored hashed like passwords.
